name: Illusion of asymmetric insight
statement: People believe they know their friends, their roommates and rival groups better than those others know them, because they take their own nature to be the harder one to read.
meaning: Pronin, Kruger, Savitsky and Ross put three claims on the table. The first is interpersonal: I know you better than you know me. The second is intrapersonal: I know myself better than you know yourself. The third follows from the other two, and says the gap between what a person knows about himself and what others know about him is wider for the self than for anyone else. The mechanism they propose is a rule about what counts as evidence. Overt behaviour is treated as diagnostic when somebody else produces it and as noise when one produces it oneself, while private thoughts and feelings are treated as diagnostic of the self alone. On that account the claim is not that one perceives more sharply. It is that one is harder to perceive. Two neighbouring entries carry material that is not repeated here. The framework that explains the asymmetry by how heavily people weigh their own introspections is the introspection illusion, entry 167. The self-other gap in admitted susceptibility to named biases is the bias blind spot, entry 133.

origin.who: Emily Pronin, Justin Kruger, Kenneth Savitsky and Lee Ross
origin.where: Journal of Personality and Social Psychology
origin.note: The paper that names the effect and reports six studies, five on person perception and one on groups. Its samples run from 17 dyads to 200 students. It prints t and F statistics and no standardised effect size for any of its self-other comparisons.

evidence: The six studies ran on undergraduates at Williams College, the University of Illinois and Stanford. In Study 1, 125 students rated a close friend on 11-point scales. They said they knew the friend, M = 8.89, better than the friend knew them, M = 8.64, t(124) = 2.26, p < .03, and 48 claimed the advantage against 24 who claimed the reverse, Z = 2.83, p < .005. Asked to circle one of ten partly submerged icebergs, they placed themselves deeper, 7.67 against 8.02 for the friend, t(124) = 3.19, p < .003. Study 2 gave 45 same-sex roommate pairs a 12-item composite on 9-point scales. Participants rated their knowledge of the roommate at 5.74 and the roommate's knowledge of them at 5.50, t(44) = 2.96, p < .005, and their own self-knowledge at 7.39 against the roommate's 6.70, t(44) = 5.54, p < .0001. The gap between their own self-knowledge and their roommate's knowledge of them, 1.89, exceeded the mirror-image gap of 0.97, t(44) = 5.51, p < .0001. That asymmetry was wider for private domains, 0.33, than public ones, 0.06, t(44) = 2.26, p < .05, and wider among pairs who were not close friends, 2.16 against 1.53, F(1, 42) = 5.04, p < .05. In Study 3, 200 students completed the sentence 'I am most like myself when I ...' for themselves and once for a friend. Two blind raters coded 72% of the completely private answers as being about the self and 66% of the answers naming contexts visible to intimates as being about the friend, chi-square(1, N = 200) = 17.45, p < .001. Study 4 brought together 17 previously unacquainted same-sex dyads. After a minute of conversation the asymmetry was marginal, 3.04 against 2.90, t(16) = 2.01, p < .10. After a 20-question exchange it reached 5.30 against 5.05, t(16) = 3.35, p < .005, and participants wrote 14.6 lines on what they had learned against 11.0 lines on what their partner had learned, t(16) = 4.93, p < .0001. Study 5 recruited 21 male and 13 female Stanford undergraduates, 18 of whom completed and rated their own word fragments first and 16 of whom rated a peer's first. They rated the peer's completions as more revealing than their own, t(30) = 2.29, p < .03 on the 21-item composite. Explaining their inferences, they quoted 3.94 of the partner's completions on average and 1.23 of their own, t(30) = 4.02, p < .0001. Study 6 asked 80 students about liberals and conservatives, pro-choice and pro-life advocates, and women and men. Each pairing produced a difference between the two groups' answers in the predicted direction, F(1, 65) = 6.22, F(1, 74) = 7.09 and F(1, 77) = 4.04.

replication.headline: The asymmetry turned up again in Korean and American samples, both read only through their abstracts, and neither a preregistered attempt nor a reported failure was located.
replication.detail: Park, Choi and Cho ran three studies on Korean participants. Their abstract reports that the asymmetry was present in Study 1, that Study 2 found it to be a bias rather than an accurate report, and that Study 3 traced part of it to how people judge the situational variability of their own behaviour against other people's. Cho, Otani, Han and Van Horn then compared American students, 114 men and 192 women, with Korean students, 99 men and 98 women. Their abstract reports asymmetry on all three of their items, Know, Understand and Visibility, in horizontal relationships with best friends and in vertical relationships with parents, and greater asymmetry in the Korean group than the American group on Understand and Visibility. Neither full text was obtained, so this entry carries no replication effect size, no test statistic and no interval, and nothing about how either study was analysed. Park and colleagues' article is closed at SAGE, and Seoul National University's open repository and its Pure record both hold the item with no file attached. Cho and colleagues' article is closed at Taylor and Francis, whose page answers this session with a bot challenge, and Central Michigan University's repository refused the connection at the egress proxy. Unpaywall, OpenAlex and Semantic Scholar record both as closed. Pronin came back to the mechanism herself seven years later. In Study 4 of Pronin, Fleming and Steffel, 56 Princeton undergraduates disclosed an important value to a stranger and then answered 20 projective statements, with the dyad as the unit of analysis. Speakers held their own value disclosures to be more revealing than their partner's, 5.23 against 4.67, F(1, 27) = 6.12, p = .02. The reverse pattern for projective responses, which is the Study 5 mechanism of 2001, reached 2.38 against 2.61, F(1, 27) = 3.79, p = .06, and so fell short of significance. The interaction the authors predicted held, F(1, 27) = 10.31, p = .003. Searches ran on 21 September 2026 across Crossref, PubMed, Europe PMC, OpenAlex, Unpaywall, Semantic Scholar's 180 citing papers for the 2001 article, OSF preprints and registrations, and the open web. They turned up no preregistered test of any part of the effect and no reported failure. One further lead was found and not read: Crossref carries a 2005 PsycEXTRA record by Takeda and Numazaki on relationship intimacy and the illusion of asymmetric insight, with no abstract, no pagination and no venue, and the APA site that holds it answers with a bot challenge.

study.cite: Cho, Y., Otani, H., Han, K., & Van Horn, K. R. (2010). Cultural differences in asymmetric beliefs of interpersonal knowledge in vertical and horizontal relationships. The Journal of General Psychology, 137(4), 343-361.

limits: The original evidence is thin study by study and consistent across studies. Its six samples were 125 students, 45 roommate pairs, 200 students, 17 dyads, 21 men and 13 women, and 80 students, drawn from three American colleges. Study 5's tests carry 30 degrees of freedom, and the article names no exclusion that would account for the gap from the number it recruited. None was preregistered. Every study asks one person about both self and other, which tells participants what is being compared. Study 6 does this in the open: a footnote records that all items for a given pair of groups appeared together, which the authors say made the comparison, and possibly the object of the investigation, explicit. Study 5 held in only one order. Participants who rated a peer's word completions before producing their own saw the peer's as more revealing, 3.54 against 2.93, t(18) = 2.95, p < .009, while those who rated their own first saw no difference, 2.86 against 2.92, t < 1, interaction F(1, 30) = 5.19, p < .03. The authors read that as doing the task teaching people to doubt word completions in general. The measures are beliefs about knowledge rather than knowledge. In Study 2 the roommate design sets two people's claims against each other, which shows the pair cannot both be right without showing which one is wrong, and Park and colleagues' abstract is the only located source that claims to have tested the beliefs against accuracy. Pronin's own later work bounds the mechanism. In Pronin, Fleming and Steffel, speakers rated their disclosures of important values as more revealing than their partner's, which is the opposite sign to Study 5, and the authors describe the two effects as a flipside of each other. Their reading is that a value feels intensely held and therefore diagnostic to the person holding it, while an off-the-cuff response feels random.
misreadings: The intergroup finding is usually retold as each side believing it understands the other better. The group means do not carry that. Liberals put their knowledge of conservatives at 5.81 against 5.14 the other way, t(34) = 3.10, p < .005, while conservatives gave 5.13 against 5.01, t(31) < 1. Pro-choice participants gave 5.42 against 4.47, t(53) = 4.09, p < .0001, and pro-life participants 5.30 against 5.01, t(21) < 1. Women and men both said women know men better, women putting the gap at 0.96, t(38) = 4.04, p < .0005, and men at 0.38, t(39) = 2.18, p < .05. What reached significance in each pairing is the difference between the two groups' answers, not a matching illusion held by each of them. The second misreading is one of scale. In Study 1 the two means sit a quarter of a point apart on an 11-point scale, and the authors write that the mean differences were small in absolute terms. Study 4's longer session gives 5.30 against 5.05 on a 9-point scale, and a footnote attributes the p value to a small within-subject error term rather than to a large difference. The third is that this is ordinary self-flattery, or the bias blind spot under a new name. Pronin and colleagues tested the first directly. Their roommates rated themselves as more competitive than their partners, 6.72 against 5.60, t(44) = 4.98, p < .0001, and as looking in the mirror more often, 6.16 against 5.03, t(44) = 4.78, p < .0001, neither of which flatters anybody. The blind spot, entry 133, is a different measurement. It asks how susceptible one is to named biases, and it has preregistered direct replications with pooled estimates. This asks who knows whom, and no preregistered replication of it was located.

sources.text: Pronin, E., Kruger, J., Savitsky, K., & Ross, L. (2001). You don't know me, but I know you: The illusion of asymmetric insight. Journal of Personality and Social Psychology, 81(4), 639-656. Read in full from the first author's posted copy; the source for every figure in the evidence, limits and misreadings sections. Crossref records the third author's surname as 'Savtisky', and Princeton's record of the paper reverses the second and third authors and gives the last page as 655; the printed article's own header gives 639-656.

Park, J., Choi, I., & Cho, G. (2006). The actor-observer bias in beliefs of interpersonal insights. Journal of Cross-Cultural Psychology, 37(6), 630-642. Closed at SAGE. The abstract was read from Seoul National University's open repository record, which states that no file is attached, and the same abstract appears on the university's Pure record. No figure from the article appears on this page.

Cho, Y., Otani, H., Han, K., & Van Horn, K. R. (2010). Cultural differences in asymmetric beliefs of interpersonal knowledge in vertical and horizontal relationships. The Journal of General Psychology, 137(4), 343-361. Closed at Taylor and Francis, which answers this session with a bot challenge rather than a paywall page. The abstract was read from PubMed's XML, and the counts quoted here are the ones it prints. The article gives no combined total for either national sample, so none is printed here.

Steglich-Petersen, A., & Skipper, M. (2019). Explaining the illusion of asymmetric insight. Review of Philosophy and Psychology, 10(4), 769-786. A philosophical reanalysis with no new data, which argues that existing explanations of the illusion either invert the explanatory direction or fit the experiments too loosely. An open-access copy is deposited at PhilPapers and both Unpaywall and Semantic Scholar record it as green open access, but philpapers.org and philarchive.org answer this session with a Cloudflare challenge and Springer with a JavaScript client challenge. Only the abstract and the bibliographic line were obtained, from Aarhus University's Pure record. Crossref's entry for the article carries no volume, issue or pages.

Pronin, E., Fleming, J. J., & Steffel, M. (2008). Value revelations: Disclosure is in the eye of the beholder. Journal of Personality and Social Psychology, 95(4), 795-809. Read in full from two copies, the third author's posted copy and the first author's, which are the same file. Six experiments by the original first author; Study 4 is the source for the figures quoted from it here.
